intro: In this college you'll learn to talk about your home in Dutch: name the types of homes and the rooms, describe your furniture, say exactly where things are, handle the language of renting and living independently, and write a short note to your neighbours.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome home
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme five. Its title is [[Dit is mijn huis]], which means 'this is my house'. Your home is where Dutch life really happens, and you will talk about it more than you expect: with neighbours, with a landlord, with friends you invite over. So let's start with the building itself. A house is [[het huis]], and a flat or apartment is [[het appartement]]. Notice the little word [[het]] in front of both; Dutch has two words for 'the', either [[de]] or [[het]], and sadly you simply have to learn which one goes with each noun. A useful rule of thumb: most words are [[de]] words, so when you are unsure, guess [[de]]. To say where you live, use [[Ik woon in een appartement]], 'I live in an apartment'. Many people live upstairs, so you will hear [[op de tweede verdieping]], meaning 'on the second floor'. And the warmest Dutch word for a home that feels nice and snug is [[gezellig]] — there is no perfect English translation, but it means cosy, sociable and welcoming all at once. When you walk into a friend's place, a lovely thing to say is [[Wat een gezellig huis!]], 'what a cosy house!'. Let's go inside.

paragraphs.heading: A tour of the rooms
paragraphs.text: Let's walk through the rooms one by one. As you open the door, you can point and say [[Dit is de woonkamer]], 'this is the living room'. The kitchen is [[de keuken]], and you might add [[en daar is de keuken]], 'and over there is the kitchen'. Where you sleep is [[de slaapkamer]], the bedroom, and where you wash is [[de badkamer]], the bathroom. A handy general word for any room is [[de kamer]]. If you are lucky, there is also [[de tuin]], the garden, or perhaps a small [[balkon]], a balcony. To ask about a home's size, the question is [[Hoeveel kamers heeft je huis?]], which means 'how many rooms does your house have?'. You answer simply, for example [[Mijn huis heeft vier kamers.]] A very natural way to describe your favourite spot is [[Mijn slaapkamer kijkt uit op de tuin]], meaning 'my bedroom looks out over the garden'. Notice that all these room words take [[de]]: [[de woonkamer]], [[de keuken]], [[de slaapkamer]]. But the bed itself is a [[het]] word, [[het bed]], and so is the house, [[het huis]]. Try saying your own little tour out loud now, walking from room to room and naming each one in Dutch.

paragraphs.heading: Furniture and saying what there is
paragraphs.text: Now let's fill those rooms with furniture, which in Dutch is [[de meubels]]. The most useful pieces are [[de tafel]], the table; [[de stoel]], the chair; [[het bed]], the bed; and [[de kast]], the cupboard or wardrobe. To say what a room contains, Dutch loves the little word [[er]], meaning 'there'. With one thing you say [[er is]], and a beautiful example is [[Er is een grote tuin achter het huis]], 'there is a big garden behind the house'. With more than one thing you say [[er zijn]], as in [[Er zijn drie slaapkamers in dit appartement]], 'there are three bedrooms in this apartment'. To ask, you simply turn it around: [[Is er een lift in het gebouw?]] means 'is there a lift in the building?'. And to say something is missing, use [[geen]], for example [[Er zijn geen meubels in de woonkamer]], 'there is no furniture in the living room'. This pattern with [[er is]] and [[er zijn]] is one of the most practical things in this whole theme, because it lets you describe any home, any room and anything you are looking for. Practise it with your own house: what [[er is]] in your living room right now?

paragraphs.heading: Exactly where things are
paragraphs.text: Once you can say what there is, you want to say exactly where it is, and for that Dutch uses small position words. The key ones are [[op]], meaning 'on'; [[in]], meaning 'in'; [[naast]], 'next to'; [[onder]], 'under'; and [[boven]], 'above'. Here is the lovely Dutch twist: instead of a flat verb 'to be', Dutch usually picks a verb that shows the position. Things that stand upright use [[er staat]], from the verb 'to stand'; flat things that lie down use [[er ligt]], 'to lie'; and anything on the wall uses [[er hangt]], 'to hang'. So you might say [[De lamp hangt boven de tafel]], 'the lamp hangs above the table'; or [[De schoenen staan naast de deur]], 'the shoes stand next to the door'. A cat resting on the floor gives us [[De kat ligt onder de bank]], 'the cat lies under the sofa'. And combining two positions: [[Het boek ligt op het bureau in de slaapkamer]], 'the book lies on the desk in the bedroom'. Don't worry about choosing the perfect verb at first; people will understand you. But the more you copy [[er staat]], [[er ligt]] and [[er hangt]], the more your Dutch will sound truly natural and at home.

paragraphs.heading: Renting and living on your own
paragraphs.text: In the Netherlands many people rent, so the language of renting is essential. The rent is [[de huur]], and your landlord is [[de huisbaas]]. To ask the price, say [[Hoeveel is de huur per maand?]], 'how much is the rent per month?'. A typical answer is [[De huur is 750 euro per maand]], 'the rent is 750 euros a month'. Often the price includes utilities, gas, water and electricity, which Dutch sums up as [[inclusief gas, water en licht]]. If you are searching for a place, a key sentence is [[Ik zoek een kamer in het centrum]], 'I am looking for a room in the centre'. When you want to view it, ask politely [[Mag ik het huis even bekijken?]], 'may I have a quick look at the house?'. You may hear that a room is [[gemeubileerd]], furnished, or that you share with others, [[Er is een gedeelde keuken en badkamer]], 'there is a shared kitchen and bathroom'. When you move house, the verb is [[verhuizen]], as in [[Wij gaan volgende maand verhuizen]], 'we are going to move next month'. A practical tip: always ask for a written contract, [[een huurcontract]], and never pay large sums in cash. Knowing these words protects you and gives you real confidence.

paragraphs.heading: A note to the neighbours
paragraphs.text: Let's finish where Dutch home life truly lives: with the neighbours. Good neighbours are gold, and the Dutch describe them warmly: [[De buren zijn aardig en rustig]], 'the neighbours are nice and quiet'. When you move in, it is a lovely custom to introduce yourself or leave a short note. Imagine you slip a card through the letterbox. You could write: [[Hallo, wij zijn uw nieuwe buren.]] [[Wij wonen nu naast u, op nummer 12.]] [[Sorry voor het geluid, wij gaan deze week verhuizen.]] That last line apologises for the noise of moving in. You might also invite them: [[Kom gerust een keer langs voor een kopje koffie!]], 'feel free to drop by for a cup of coffee!'. And if you ever hear knocking at your own door, you can warmly say [[Doe alsof je thuis bent]], 'make yourself at home'. There is even a cosy Dutch proverb: [[Oost west, thuis best]], meaning 'east, west, home is best' — there's no place like home. So this week, practise describing your own home out loud, room by room, and write one friendly line to a neighbour. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done — and I'll see you in theme six!
